Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 32, verse 5–9:

Allah's words: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of this verse. The first: He decrees the decree from the heaven, and sends it down to the earth with the angels; ﴿then it ascends to Him﴾ by the angel, ﴿in a Day﴾ of the days of this world. So the angel covers, in one day of the days of this world, in its descent and its ascent, a distance of a thousand years of a human's journey.

The second: He arranges the affair of this world for the duration of the days of this world, so the decree and the destiny descend from the heaven to the earth, ﴿then it ascends to Him﴾, meaning the affair and the arrangement return to Him when the orders of the rulers and the judgments of the judges end, and Allah the Exalted stands alone in the affair, ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾. This is on the Day of Resurrection, because each day of the days of the Hereafter is like a thousand years.

Mujahid said: He decrees the affair of a thousand years in one day, then He casts it to the angels; when it has passed, He decrees for another thousand years, and so on forever.

Regarding what is meant by "the affair" (al-amr), the exegetes have three opinions. The first: it is the revelation (al-wahy), said by al-Suddi. The second: it is the decree (al-qada'), said by Muqatil. The third: it is the affairs of this world.

﴿Ya'ruju﴾ means "yas'adu" (ascends). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "'araja fi al-sullam a'raju" (I climbed the ladder), and "'araja al-rajulu ya'raju" (the man became lame) when he became a lame person.

Mu'adh al-Qari', Ibn al-Sumayfa', and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "thumma yu'raju ilayhi" with a raised yā' and an opened rā'. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited: "ya'riju" with an opened yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited: "thumma ta'ruju" with an opened tā' and a raised rā'.

Allah's words: ﴿He who made everything He created good﴾. In this there are five opinions.

The first: He made it good. The second: He made everything firm and sound; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and the first was said by Qatadah, and the second by Mujahid. The third: He made it well, meaning He taught it to no one; as one says, "Fulan yuhsinu kadha" (so-and-so does such-and-such well) when he knows it; this was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. The fourth: the meaning is that He inspired His creation with everything they need, as if He informed them of all of that and perfected them; this was said by al-Farra'. The fifth: He did good to everything He created; this is related by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His words ﴿khalaqahu﴾ (what He created) there are two readings. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir recited "khalqahu" with a silent lam. The rest recited it with a vowelled lam. Al-Zajjaj said: Its opening (with a fatha on the lam) is as a past verb, and its sukun is as an apposition (badal), so the meaning becomes: He perfected the creation of everything He created. Abu 'Ubayda said: The meaning is: He perfected the creation of everything; the Arabs do such things, placing words forward and backward.

Allah's words: ﴿And He began the creation of man﴾, meaning Adam; ﴿then He made his offspring﴾, that is, his descendants and progeny. The explanation of this verse has already passed [al-Mu'minun: 12].

Then He returned to Adam and said: ﴿Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾. Its explanation has already passed [al-Hijr: 29]. Then He returned to his descendants and said: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight﴾, that is, after you were drops of semen.

[Note: the dot-marked ḍād] vowelled with a fatḥa and the first lām with a kasra. Al-Farrāʾ said: "ḍalilnā" and "ḍalalnā" are two dialects, and the meaning is: when our bones and flesh have become dust (p-336) like the earth. One says: "ḍalla al-māʾ fī al-laban" (the water got lost/mixed into the milk) and "ḍalla al-shayʾ fī al-shayʾ" (the thing was lost/hidden in the thing) when it conceals it and overcomes it. Abū Nuhayk, Abū al-Mutawakkil, Abū al-Jawzāʾ, Abū Ḥaywa and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "ḍulilnā" (ضُلِّلْنا) with a ḍamma on the ḍād and a shadda on the first lām, with a kasra. ﴿They call upon their Lord in fear﴾ of His punishment ﴿and in hope﴾ of His mercy [and His reward] ﴿and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ in obligatory and voluntary charity.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 32, verse 23–30:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, ﴿so do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

The first: "So do not be in doubt about Moses' meeting with his Lord." This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second: "about Moses' meeting [on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey)]." This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: "so do not be in doubt about meeting affliction, as Moses met [it]." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: "Do not be in doubt about Moses' receiving the Book of Allah with acceptance and approval." This was said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: It has also been said: "So do not be in doubt about Moses' meeting the Book," so that the pronoun refers to the Book. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The meaning is "Moses' meeting the Book," and the verbal noun is attributed to the pronoun referring to the Book. In this there is praise for him for complying with what he was commanded, and an exhortation to take up the same kind of action.

Regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a guidance﴾ there are two opinions. One: the Book, said by al-Hasan. The second: Moses, said by Qatadah.

﴿And We made from among them﴾, that is, from among the Children of Israel, ﴿leaders (a'immah)﴾, that is, guides in goodness, ﴿guiding by Our command﴾, that is, calling people to obedience to Allah, ﴿when they were patient﴾ [Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "lamma sabaru" with a fathah on the lam and a shaddah on the mim. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "li-ma" with a kasrah on the lam and no shaddah. Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-ma" with a ba' in place of the lam; the meaning is their patience] in their religion and in the harm of their enemies, ﴿and they were certain of Our signs﴾ that they are from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Regarding them there are two opinions: one, that they were the prophets; the second, that they were righteous people other than the prophets. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh: if you obey, I will make leaders from among you.

His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord — He will judge between them﴾, that is, He will decide and rule. Regarding those referred to there are two opinions: one, that they are the prophets and their nations; the second, the believers and the polytheists.

Then He threatened the disbelievers of Makkah by His saying: ﴿Did it not guide them?﴾ Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "nahdi" with a nun. Its interpretation has already passed in (Ta-Ha: 128).

﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water﴾, meaning the rain and the torrent, ﴿to the barren land﴾, which is the land that does not grow vegetation (we have mentioned it at the beginning of al-Kahf: 8). When the water comes, it causes to grow therein what people and livestock eat.

﴿And they say﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿When is this victory?﴾ Regarding this there are four opinions.

One: it is that which was not opened on the day of Badr. 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this verse that he said: On the day of Badr, victory was opened for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the faith of those who disbelieved did not benefit them after death.

The second: it is the Day of Resurrection, which is the day of judgment with reward and punishment, said by Mujahid.

The third: it is the day on which the punishment will come to them in this world; said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: the conquest of Makkah, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutaybah. This view has been objected to, and it was said: How would the faith of the disbelievers not benefit them on the day of the conquest, when a group embraced Islam and their Islam was accepted that day? In answer to this there are two responses.

One: the faith after death does not benefit those among the disbelievers who were killed that day; this has been mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas. The people of biography have mentioned that Khalid entered on the day of the conquest from a different route from the one by which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered, and Safwan ibn Umayyah and Suhayl ibn 'Amr, along with others, met him and fought him. Khalid cried out to his companions and fought them, and he killed twenty-four men of Quraysh and four of Hudhayl, and they fled. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became aware, he said: "Did I not forbid fighting?" It was said: Khalid was attacked and so he fought back.

The second: the protection that they were given does not benefit the disbelievers, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe." Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "amantu fulanan iman," so according to this the meaning is that this protection does not repel from them the punishment of Allah. This opinion which we have defended is not the preferred one; we have only explained its basis because it has been said.

Besides what we have mentioned about the victory, there are two opinions: one, that it means judgment and decision, which is what we choose; the second, the conquest of the land.

His saying: ﴿So turn away from them and wait﴾, that is, wait for their punishment, ﴿indeed they are waiting﴾ for the vicissitudes of time to befall you. The exegetes said: This verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.
